title: Fractional-GPU cgroup enforcement and speculative eviction for noisy-tenant mitigation
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Implement a new enforcement layer that supports fractional GPU allocations via OS cgroups + MIG-awareness, combined with a speculative eviction mechanism that performs gradual workload dampening instead of hard kills. Goal is to reduce cross-tenant interference that causes downstream P95/P99 latency spikes while preserving tenant throughput contracts and burst credits.
background: We continue to see regressing tail latency for some tenants on shared racks during mixed workloads (long context generation + short chat). Existing hard-eviction policies cause customer pain: sudden request failures and long cold-restarts for large-model workloads. Current solutions (static hard slices or aggressive preemption) trade availability for isolation. We need a mechanism that enforces throughput contracts more smoothly and allows autoscaler to reclaim capacity predictably without high customer-visible failure rates.
proposed_solution: 1) Introduce a cgroup-based fractional GPU enforcement shim (daemon) per host that maps tenant throughput contracts to cgroup cpu/mem/io equivalents for the GPU driver where supported, and respects MIG partitions when GPUs expose MIG slices. 2) Implement a token-bucket per-tenant ‘throughput wallet’ representing GPU-time units; when exhausted, instead of immediate eviction, the shim applies progressive backpressure (reduce CUDA stream priority, throttle kernel launch rate, and lower per-request concurrency) — called speculative eviction. 3) Integrate the spec-evict signals with the autoscaler so that when tokens are low and queues persist, the autoscaler increases dedicated capacity or shifts load to fallback model variants. 4) Expose metrics and a small API to surface wallet state, throttle reasons, and predicted time-to-recover so Console can show live tenant health and for use in runbooks.
acceptance_criteria:
- Hosts deploy shim in canary rack and report per-tenant token-bucket metrics to Prometheus.
- Under synthetic mixed workloads, P95 and P99 for low-latency tenants improve by at least 30% compared to the current hard-evict baseline.
- No silent request drops: speculative eviction must return graceful 429s or slow responses rather than process termination.
- Autoscaler reacts to spec-evict metrics within existing scaling windows and avoids oscillation in 90% of test runs.
- Console shows wallet balance and throttle reason for canary tenants.
tradeoffs:
- Pros: smoother degradation, fewer customer-visible failures, better SLO adherence for latency-sensitive tenants.
- Cons: added complexity in host daemon and driver interaction; may not be feasible on older GPU drivers or non-MIG hardware. Potential for subtle performance regressions if throttle heuristics are not tuned. Additional telemetry and rank-ordering logic required to prevent gaming of token-buckets.
test_plan:
1) Unit tests for token-bucket accounting and state transitions.
2) Hardware-in-the-loop canary on two racks: run combinations of long-context LLM generations and short chat workloads; measure latency distributions.
3) Chaos test: simulate node GPU flakiness and ensure fallback without request loss.
4) Autoscale integration tests that verify policy triggers and no thrashing across 50+ scale events.
5) Regression suite comparing cost-per-token with and without shim across 7 workloads.
rollout_plan:
- Phase 0 (dev): local host tests and driver compatibility matrix. (1 week)
- Phase 1 (alpha): Deploy daemon to one canary rack with 5 tenants flagged for experiment. Monitor for 2 weeks.
- Phase 2 (beta): Expand to 20% of fleet, expose Console metrics and opt-in API. Run traffic shaping tests for 4 weeks.
- Phase 3 (ga): Auto-enable on Dedicated clusters with release feature flag off by default, provide opt-in per-tenant, enable by default after 6 weeks if SLOs stable.
